introduction: From the 1870s Bahá’u’lláh, and after him ‘Abdu’l-Bahá in the West, proposed a Supreme Tribunal: a court elected through the parliaments of all nations, to which disputes between states would be referred, whose judgments all would be bound to uphold, and against whose defiers all would act. The guide follows the proposal through talks given on the eve of the First World War, a letter of hope to the League of Nations, and later statements that deliberately leave its relation to a world state undefined. The prophets saw it first as a hope: “he shall judge among the nations”. Kant, Tennyson and Wilson gave it modern forms; Deuteronomy’s higher court, the Gospel’s steps for settling a quarrel, and the Qur’an’s rule for restraining an aggressor are its small-scale models. Hobbes states the problem it must solve, Jefferson the fear of entanglement that kept a great power out, and Madison and Acton the question every such plan must face: who controls the controller.
questions: The Qur’an’s rule is to make peace, and if one party wrongs the other, to oppose the wrongdoer until it returns. How does reading 12 apply the same logic to nations, and what would it require of each?
Hobbes thought only a common power ends the war of all against all. Kant feared a single world power. Where between them do readings 21 and 22 stand?
Jefferson warned against entangling alliances. What must a nation believe before it will submit its own cause to a tribunal?
Madison says a government must be obliged to control itself, and Acton that power corrupts. What safeguards do the readings name, and which do they leave to be worked out (27 to 29)?
Reading 2 makes the Tribunal conditional on peace-lovers becoming numerous. Which has to come first, the institution or the will?

outside.why: A Supreme Tribunal established by peoples and governments. Isaiah: he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people: and they shall beat their swords into plowshares.
Tennyson’s lines of 1842, which ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s hearers knew: till the war-drum throbb’d no longer, and the battle-flags were furl’d in the Parliament of man, the Federation of the world.

The Tribunal is “conditional” on peace-lovers becoming numerous. UNESCO’s founders said why: since wars begin in the minds of men, it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be constructed.

Nations and governments must organize an international body. Kant in 1795 proposed a federation of free states, and preferred it to a single world monarchy, which he thought would end as a soulless despotism.

Differences are to be “amicably and conclusively settled”. Israel’s law provides a higher court: if there arise a matter too hard for thee in judgment, thou shalt come unto the judge that shall be in those days, and do according to the sentence.
Each nation elects representatives. Jethro’s counsel to Moses: provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness.

Its members are to be chosen “from among the wiser and most judicious”. Plato thought cities would have no rest until philosophers ruled, and knew that the wise seldom want office. How do readings 5, 6, 19 and 20 propose to find and bind such people?
Universal peace as a principle. Nation shall not lift up a sword against nation; they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree.
An international tribunal to arbitrate all disputes. The Gospel’s procedure for a quarrel between two has the same steps: go to him alone; then take witnesses; then tell it unto the assembly.

It would go further than the Hague tribunal. Woodrow Wilson’s fourteenth point, six years after this talk: a general association of nations must be formed under specific covenants for mutual guarantees of independence and integrity to great and small states alike.
An international tongue will be used in its work. Then will I turn to the people a pure language, that they may all call upon the name of the Lord, to serve him with one consent.

All must obey its decisions; a nation that defies them is to be resisted by all. The Qur’an’s rule for two parties of believers: make peace between them; and if one party doeth wrong to the other, fight ye that which doeth wrong till it return.

Hobbes held that where there is no common power to keep all in awe, there is war of every man against every man, and life is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. He thought nations stand to each other in that condition. The readings propose the common power. What would make states accept it?
Questions national and international are referred to it. The psalm of the unjust judges ends: arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá hopes the League will become a Supreme Tribunal. Jefferson’s inaugural gave his country its contrary maxim for a century: peace, commerce, and honest friendship with all nations, entangling alliances with none. The United States stayed out of the League. What does a nation fear to lose?

New inventions deepened “the law of co-operation”. The same inventions made 1914. Wilfred Owen: what passing-bells for these who die as cattle? Only the monstrous anger of the guns. Why did the arts of cooperation not prevent it?
Had Austria and Serbia gone to a general tribunal, it would have judged between the strong and the weak. Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy.
Two or three from each country, the best in competence and character. In the multitude of counsellors there is safety.

Elected by parliaments and confirmed by every organ of the state. Burke on what a representative owes once chosen: parliament is a deliberative assembly of one nation, with one interest, that of the whole. The Tribunal asks its members for the same enlargement, to the world.

“Some form of a world super-state”, to which nations cede the right to make war. Madison: in framing a government you must first enable it to control the governed, and in the next place oblige it to control itself. Who obliges a world state?

Acton’s rule gives no exemption for size: power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely. What in the readings’ design (election, representation of all, the limits they leave unspecified) answers the fear of a single power over the earth?
A commonwealth in which nations keep their autonomy and personal freedom is safeguarded. Kallen’s image for such a union: an orchestra, each people its own instrument.
The Tribunal’s membership is not closed to women by any scriptural text. The women at Seneca Falls in 1848 amended a famous sentence: all men and women are created equal.
Peace organized in a tribunal to which political questions are referred. Let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
How the Tribunal will stand to a world state “we cannot at present foresee”. The secret things belong unto the Lord our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us.
Its nature and scope are left to be worked out. A state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation.

shortfall: Several readings repeat the proposal in nearly the same words, or are brief notes on terms; they share companions.
